original_interpretation: Gartner's preliminary estimate (February 2025) put 2024 worldwide semiconductor revenue at US$626 billion, up 18.1%.

evidence_found: 'This class includes:' - manufacture of capacitors, electronic; resistors, electronic; microprocessors; bare printed circuit boards; electronic connectors; integrated circuits (analog, digital or hybrid); diodes, transistors and related discrete devices; inductors; dice or wafers, semiconductor; display components (plasma, polymer, LCD); light emitting diodes (LED); loading of components onto printed circuit boards (UNSD ISIC Rev.4 class 2610, explanatory note)
notes: web_extract returned only the page header; full text read in browser.
original_interpretation: ISIC Rev.4 class 2610 (Manufacture of electronic components and boards) groups integrated circuits, microprocessors, diodes and transistors and semiconductor wafers together with electronic capacitors, resistors, inductors, connectors, bare printed circuit boards, LCD/plasma display components, LEDs and the loading of components onto printed circuit boards.

evidence_found: 'This class excludes:' - "printing of smart cards, see 1811"; "manufacture of computer and television displays, see 2620, 2640"; "manufacture of complete equipment is classified elsewhere based on complete equipment classification" (UNSD ISIC Rev.4 2610)
original_interpretation: ISIC Rev.4 class 2610 excludes manufacture of computer and television displays and printing of smart cards; complete equipment is classified elsewhere.

evidence_found: 334410 illustrative examples include: "capacitors, electronic, fixed and variable, manufacturing"; "integrated microcircuits, manufacturing"; "loaded computer boards, manufacturing"; "printed circuit laminates, manufacturing"; "semiconductor devices (e.g., wafers), manufacturing"; "solar cells, manufacturing"; "transistors, manufacturing" (Statistics Canada, NAICS Canada 2022 v1.0, 334410)
notes: This is the Canadian NAICS (334410 is a Canadian/MEX 6-digit industry); the US 6-digit split differs (334412-334419).
original_interpretation: The Canadian NAICS 2022 industry 334410 (Semiconductor and other electronic component manufacturing) lists as illustrative examples electronic capacitors, integrated microcircuits, solar cells, printed circuit laminates, semiconductor wafers, transistors and loaded computer boards.

evidence_found: 12.(a)(i) "Semiconductor devices" are semiconductor devices the operation of which depends on variations in resistivity on the application of an electric field or semiconductor-based transducers. (Schedule B 2022, Chapter 85, Note 12)
notes: Schedule B reproduces the HS 2022 legal note; read in browser (web_extract returned only navigation).
original_interpretation: The Harmonized System (Chapter 85, Note 12) defines semiconductor devices as devices whose operation depends on variations in resistivity on the application of an electric field, or semiconductor-based transducers.

evidence_found: 12.(b) "Electronic integrated circuits" are: (i) Monolithic integrated circuits ... (ii) Hybrid integrated circuits ... (iii) Multichip integrated circuits ... (iv) Multi-component integrated circuits (MCOs) ... (Schedule B 2022, Chapter 85, Note 12(b))
original_interpretation: For customs purposes (HS heading 8542), electronic integrated circuits comprise monolithic, hybrid, multichip and multi-component integrated circuits (MCOs).

evidence_found: 12.(a)(ii) "Light-emitting diodes (LED)" are semiconductor devices based on semiconductor materials which convert electrical energy into visible, infra-red or ultra-violet rays (Schedule B 2022, Chapter 85, Note 12)
original_interpretation: The Harmonized System classifies light-emitting diodes as semiconductor devices.

correction: The statutory definition is verified, but it defines covered entities by their ability to finance/build such facilities (not 'by facilities'), and it only makes materials and equipment facilities eligible for CHIPS incentives; the statute does not say these are 'part of the semiconductor industry' - that is our interpretation. See superseding claim.
evidence_found: (2) "covered entity" means a nonprofit entity, a private entity, a consortium ... with a demonstrated ability to substantially finance, construct, expand, or modernize a facility relating to fabrication, assembly, testing, advanced packaging, production, or research and development of semiconductors, materials used to manufacture semiconductors, or semiconductor manufacturing equipment. (15 U.S.C. 4651(2))
notes: Para (2) text read on uscode.house.gov (first extract); the site then showed a maintenance page, so LII reproduction used to confirm full text.
original_interpretation: The U.S. CHIPS statute defines eligible 'covered entities' by facilities for fabrication, assembly, testing, advanced packaging, production or R&D of semiconductors, materials used to manufacture semiconductors, or semiconductor manufacturing equipment, so U.S. policy treats equipment and materials as part of the semiconductor industry.

evidence_found: "(10) The term 'mature technology node' has the meaning given the term by the Secretary." ... "(13) The term 'semiconductor' has the meaning given that term by the Secretary."; "(12) The term 'Secretary' means the Secretary of Commerce." (15 U.S.C. 4651, LII reproduction)

With the body-text figures (65% and 53%) the totals come to more than 100%. Use 50% of value added and 53% of R&D (2019). See the superseding claim.

original_interpretation: EUV light is generated by a CO2 laser firing two pulses at a fast-moving drop of tin, vaporizing it.

original_interpretation: Because EUV light is absorbed by everything including air, EUV systems use multilayer mirrors instead of lenses and keep the whole light path in high vacuum.

evidence_found: "they have a numerical aperture (NA) of 0.33. These systems print microchip features with a resolution of 13 nm, which is unreachable with deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography." (ASML EUV page, NXE systems)
original_interpretation: ASML's NXE EUV systems have a numerical aperture of 0.33 and print features with a resolution of 13 nm.

evidence_found: "Instead, the EXE uses an ingenious design: anamorphic optics. Rather than uniformly shrinking the pattern being printed, the system's mirrors demagnify it by 4x in one direction and 8x in the other. ... allowing chipmakers to continue using traditionally sized reticles." (ASML, 25 Jan 2024, section 1)

Because of this, EXE exposure fields are half the size of NXE fields. In September 2026 Intel and ASML were promoting a move to 6x12-inch masks for High NA, so 'compatibility with existing reticles' may become less central.
original_interpretation: High-NA EUV optics demagnify the mask pattern 4x in one direction and 8x in the other (anamorphic optics) to keep compatibility with existing reticles.

original_interpretation: ASML shipped the first modules of the first High-NA EUV system to Intel in December 2023.

evidence_found: "CD = k1 • λ / NA"; "k1 (or the k1 factor) is a coefficient that depends on many factors related to the chip manufacturing process. The physical limit lithography is k1 = 0.25." (ASML, The Rayleigh criterion)

original_interpretation: The smallest printable feature (critical dimension) follows the Rayleigh criterion CD = k1 x wavelength / NA, with a physical limit of k1 = 0.25.

evidence_found: "Wafers are sliced from a salami-shaped bar of 99.99% pure silicon (known as an 'ingot') and polished to extreme smoothness." (ASML, Six crucial steps, Deposition section, updated October 4, 2023)

evidence_found: "Thin films of conducting, isolating or semiconducting materials ... are deposited on the wafer"; "The wafer is then covered with a light-sensitive coating called 'photoresist'"; "the wafer may be bombarded with positive or negative ions"; "And each microchip goes through this process hundreds of times before it becomes part of a device." original_interpretation: Chipmaking repeats a loop of deposition, photoresist coating, lithography, etching and ion implantation, and a chip goes through this process hundreds of times.

evidence_found: Image caption/alt on ASML DUV page: "A close-up picture of a layer of water between our lithography system's optics and a silicon wafer." ASML story (2 Aug 2023): "adding a layer of purified water under the lens to sharpen the resolution".

evidence_found: 20-F Item 5 end-market table (US$m): "Smart Mobile Devices $ 2,678 ... Communications Infrastructure & Data Center 745 ... Home and Industrial IoT 1,189 ... Automotive 1,410 ... Non wafer revenue 769 | 652 | 117 | 17.9 % ... Total $ 6,791". Non-wafer revenue defined as "NRE services, mask production, process qualification, post-fabrication services such as bump, test, and packaging, and ... intellectual property licenses and related royalties."
original_interpretation: GlobalFoundries' 2025 non-wafer revenue (NRE, masks, qualification, bump/test/packaging services, IP licensing) was US$769 million, up 17.9%, leaving US$6,022 million of wafer revenue across its four end markets.

evidence_found: Inputs: 20-F non-wafer revenue 769 and total 6,791 (US$m); 4Q25 release Summary Annual Results "Wafer shipments (300mm equivalent) (in thousands) | 2,345 | 2,124". 20-F: "From time to time our wafer revenue consists of restructuring or underutilization payments from customers unable to meet their volume commitments."
notes: Arithmetic re-done: 6,022/2.345 = US$2,568 per wafer; 6,791/2.345 = US$2,896. The inference follows; it is not a disclosed ASP.
original_interpretation: GlobalFoundries' 2025 wafer revenue divided by wafer shipments is about US$2,570 per 300mm-equivalent wafer (US$6,022m / 2,345k), a tighter estimate than total revenue per wafer (~US$2,900); it still includes some customer restructuring or underutilization payments.

evidence_found: §231.202(a): "During the 10-year period beginning on the date of the award ... may not engage in any significant transaction involving the material expansion of semiconductor manufacturing capacity in a foreign country of concern"; 231.102 response: "CPO is removing the definition of applicable term from the rule and will instead articulate the applicable term of a particular award in the relevant award documents."; Technology Clawback "prohibits the covered entity from knowingly engaging in any joint research or technology licensing effort with a foreign entity of concern that relates to a technology or product that raises national security concerns as determined by the Secretary" (88 FR 65600)
original_interpretation: Under NIST's CHIPS guardrails final rule (15 CFR Part 231), the Expansion Clawback runs for ten years from the award date, while the Technology Clawback's term is set per award in the award documents, and it bars only knowing joint research or technology licensing with a foreign entity of concern on technologies the Secretary has flagged as raising national security concerns.

evidence_found: TSMC 7nm page: "In 2018, TSMC became the first foundry to start 7nm FinFET (N7) volume production." ... "the 7nm FinFET plus (N7+) process entered volume production in 2019 and was the first commercially available technology using EUV lithography in the foundry industry." TSMC PR 7 Oct 2019: N7+ "began volume production in the second quarter of 2019"; "original N7 process that has been in volume production for more than one year". WikiChip: "For N7, TSMC continued to use deep ultraviolet (DUV) 193 nm ArF Immersion lithography."
notes: TSMC's own (tier-1) pages establish the order (N7 in 2018, before N7+ as the first commercial EUV process), which means N7 was made without EUV. The specific statement that N7 used 193nm ArF immersion is explicit only on WikiChip (tier 3).
original_interpretation: TSMC began volume production of its first-generation 7nm (N7) process in 2018, a year before its first EUV-based process (N7+) entered volume production; N7 was patterned with 193nm ArF immersion (DUV) lithography.
